title: Images
hook: Orthodox honor icons; Catholics statues; Reformed churches keep walls plain from the second commandment

segments.voice: Yesterday, intercession: praying for one another, and the question of asking the saints. Your line was the cloud of witnesses. Who did you ask to pray, or hold in mind? Day one thousand one hundred five.

The walls of an Orthodox church look back at you. Christ, Mary, apostles and saints, painted in gold and deep color, face you from the walls and the screen before the altar. People coming in kiss the icons and light candles in front of them. Now step into a Reformed church: white walls, clear windows, a pulpit, a table, an open Bible, and very little else. Both rooms are built for prayer to the same God. Both were made to look that way on purpose. Today's word: images.

Start with the commandment. In Exodus, God says: "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above." And the next verse: don't bow down to them. Reformed churches count this as the second commandment, and they take it seriously: no images in worship, so nothing stands between the worshiper and the living God, met in his word. For them, plain walls are a form of reverence. But later in the same book, God tells Moses to make two cherubim of beaten gold for the cover of the ark. So images were not simply absent from Israel's worship. The Orthodox build on another verse. Paul calls Christ "the image of the invisible God." Their argument, made by John of Damascus when icons were under attack: the invisible God can't be painted. But when God became human, he could be seen and touched, and what can be seen can be pictured. So icons are honored, kissed and prayed before. The honor, they say, passes to the one shown; worship belongs to God alone. Catholics keep statues and paintings, crucifixes and stained glass, in a similar spirit: a picture as a way in, never the thing worshiped. Other Protestant churches sit in between, with a plain cross, or a window, or a painting of the Last Supper. So the argument isn't really whether images are good or bad. Each church is guarding something: the commandment, or the God who became visible. And each is asking what helps people pray, and what gets in the way.

Here's the practice: notice the images where you pray, or where you go to be quiet. Breathe in, and out, and let your eyes move slowly around the space. A cross, a candle, a photo of someone you love, a window, a blank wall. Or nothing at all. Ask of each thing you see: does this help me be still, or does it pull me somewhere else? Don't change anything yet. Just notice. If you pray, you can ask God for whatever helps. If you don't, let the looking be the practice. The bell holds the time.
Images. Icons, statues and pictures: honored by some churches as windows toward God, kept out by others to guard the commandment.
Your line: what helps you pray. Today, keep one thing near you that helps you be still, or clear away one thing that doesn't. Day one thousand one hundred five.

howItsDone: Orthodox Christians venerate icons at home and in church, often kissing them and lighting candles before them; Catholic churches hold statues, crucifixes and stained glass; Reformed churches keep their worship spaces plain.

fork.setup: you're defending icons. someone objects: God is invisible, so no one may picture him. how does John of Damascus answer?
options: when God became human, he could be seen, and so pictured.
fork.reveal: the invisible God can't be painted, but God made visible in Christ can. that's the heart of the case for icons.

original.note: Greek: image. Paul uses it for Christ in Colossians 1:15, "the image of the invisible God."

trapdoor: what you thought: a matter of decorating taste.
what it means: churches differ on images because they guard different things: the commandment, and the God who became visible.
what a scholar hears: Exodus forbids graven images, then orders golden cherubim for the ark; the argument over images lives between those passages and Colossians 1:15.

notes: Commandment numbering: Reformed (and Orthodox, and many others) count the images verse as the second commandment; Catholics and Lutherans fold it into the first. Only the Reformed numbering is stated; confirm.
John of Damascus's argument paraphrased (incarnation makes depiction possible); no dates or council numbers given per the claims rule.
'Other Protestant churches sit in between, with a plain cross, or a window, or a painting of the Last Supper' is descriptive and uncounted; confirm.
Orthodox church interior: 'the screen before the altar' (iconostasis) not named; confirm description.
